intro: Pachmann fits two Chopin pieces onto this 1925 HMV side: the F major Étude, Op. 25 No. 3, followed by the C♯ minor Waltz. A pianist born in 1848 meets the new electrical recording process.

sections.label: A · The F major Étude
sections.mNote: Four piano voices move in a galloping rhythm

sections.label: B · The Étude continues
sections.mNote: The hands keep their quick sideways leaps

sections.label: C · The C♯ minor Waltz
sections.mNote: Held melody notes above three-beat accompaniment

sections.label: D · Waltz melody and running quavers
sections.mNote: The right hand alternates song and quick descending phrases

sections.label: E · The Waltz’s final chords
sections.mNote: The shared record side ends in C♯ minor

cues.title: The Étude comes first
cues.text: The first piece is Chopin’s F major Étude, Op. 25 No. 3. Its hands jump sideways while four voices share the galloping rhythm. Pachmann puts it before the C♯ minor Waltz on a single HMV record side.
cues.evidence: Programme order: https://archive.org/details/hmv-db860-chopin-nocturne-no8-op27no2-etudes-op25no3-waltz-no7-op64no2. Étude’s four voices and lateral hand movements: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._3_(Chopin)

cues.title: Pachmann meets the microphone
cues.text: At Hayes on 26 June 1925, Pachmann plays his own Baldwin for HMV. These sessions produce the company’s first electrical solo-piano recordings. In December, the critic K. K. complains about the new sound in The Gramophone, yet welcomes one improvement: “he does not utter a word the whole time.”
cues.evidence: Session and instrument documentation, quoting K. K., The Gramophone, December 1925, pp. 338–39: https://archive.org/details/hmv-db860-chopin-nocturne-no8-op27no2-etudes-op25no3-waltz-no7-op64no2

cues.title: A waltz after the Étude
cues.text: The C♯ minor Waltz begins with a melody in paired notes, held across the bar line. Short curls answer it, above the left hand’s bass note and two chords. After the Étude’s bustling four voices, the piano settles into three beats.
cues.evidence: Waltz opening, Knute Snortum engraving (2023), p. 1. The established section boundary marks the change of work. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Talking at the keyboard
cues.text: Onstage, Pachmann talks before playing and sometimes while playing. At Yale, an all-Chopin recital programme announces his Baldwin piano; the inside cover advertises Steinway. Even the printed programme has room for an argument.
cues.evidence: Yale School of Music’s surviving programme and account of Pachmann’s stage manner: https://music.yale.edu/2009/04/03/from-the-archives-vladimir-de-pachmanns-all-chopin-recital-at-the-yale-school-of-music. The programme itself is undated.

cues.title: C♯ minor closes the side
cues.text: The waltz’s running tune carries the ending. Its descending quavers finally reach the C♯ minor cadence: the second piece, and the record side, end together.
cues.evidence: Score, final Più mosso and cadence, p. 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
